title: Open my lips (Psalm 51:17)
hookLine: "O Lord, open Thou my lips", the Amidah's first line

lines: THE PRAYER STARTS BY ADMITTING IT.
cards: A speech rehearsed in the car. Then the door opens, the person looks up, and nothing comes out. Or the wrong thing does.
A job interview, a hospital bed, an apology owed for a year. The words were there an hour ago. The Amidah, the central prayer of every Jewish service, starts by admitting exactly this.
Before a single blessing, the person praying asks for help just to speak.

teach.b: The line comes from Psalm 51, a psalm of a broken person asking to be made whole again. In the old Jewish translation: "O Lord, open Thou my lips; and my mouth shall declare Thy praise." In Hebrew, Adonai sefatai tiftach.
Notice the order. Not: I will praise You.

But: You open, and then my mouth will praise. Even the ability to pray is asked for, not assumed. The rabbis placed this verse right at the threshold of the Amidah, said quietly after the three steps.
But it raised a problem. Three days ago: no gap between redemption and the Amidah. So isn't this verse an interruption?
The Talmud, in Berakhot, answers: no. Since the rabbis established it as part of the prayer, it counts as one long Amidah. The verse isn't a pause before the prayer.

teach.h: NOT A GAP: THE FRONT DOOR.
teach.b: It's the prayer's front door, already inside.
The Amidah will go on to praise God as great and mighty, and to ask for wisdom, for healing, for peace.
Big words. And it begins by saying: left to myself, I might not get them out. In the prayer's picture, the speaker taps the microphone and asks someone else to switch it on.

how: Jews say Adonai sefatai tiftach, "O Lord, open my lips", quietly at the start of every Amidah, right after taking the three steps forward; it's treated as part of the Amidah itself.

o: bless my mouth, said before eating bread
open my lips, the Amidah's first words
seal my lips, a vow to keep silent

games.q: you're a rabbi of the Talmud. someone objects: this verse comes between redemption and the Amidah, so it's a gap. what do you answer?

practice: Rest your lips together and notice them, closed and quiet, and think of one sentence you'd like to say well today.
If you pray, say the psalm's line softly, O Lord, open Thou my lips; if not, hold the wish that the right words come. Then, on an out-breath, let your lips part.

wordCard.voice: Sefatai tiftach. My lips, open — the verse from Psalm fifty-one that begins the Amidah, asking for help to speak before speaking.
